topic: Strange borders: Sokh and six enclaves
hook: Your passport can say Uzbekistan while every road around you is in Kyrgyzstan.
title: 6 Places Stuck Inside Another Country (India Too)
description:
Your passport can say Uzbekistan while every road around you is in Kyrgyzstan, and that is one of six real border oddities in this countdown. From Sokh in the Fergana Valley to the Cooch Behar enclaves between India and Bangladesh, every place is on a real map. Watch to the end for India's strangest border.

#borders #geography #mapfacts

scenes.narration: Your passport can say Uzbekistan while every road around you is in Kyrgyzstan.
scenes.headline: Uzbek Inside Kyrgyzstan

scenes.narration: That is real, and it is one of six places in this video where a border makes no sense at all.
scenes.headline: 6 Impossible Borders

scenes.narration: By the end, you will see a tiny patch of India that sat inside Bangladesh, inside India, inside Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: India's Strangest

scenes.narration: We count down from six, and every place is stranger than the one before it.
scenes.headline: Countdown Starts

scenes.narration: No tricks and no made-up maps. Every place here is on a real map that you can open right now.
scenes.headline: Open Any Map App

scenes.narration: So let us start with a piece of Russia that is not connected to the rest of Russia.
scenes.headline: Start With Russia

scenes.narration: Number six: Kaliningrad, a part of Russia that has no land link to the rest of Russia.
scenes.headline: Kaliningrad

scenes.narration: Look at the map. Poland sits on one side, Lithuania on the other, and the Baltic Sea is in front.
scenes.headline: Squeezed In

scenes.narration: The rest of Russia lies far to the east, with other countries standing in between.
scenes.headline: Cut Off

scenes.narration: Its people are Russian citizens, but their neighbours on every land side are in the European Union.
scenes.headline: EU On Every Side

scenes.narration: Before 1945, this was Königsberg, a German city. After the Second World War it became Soviet.
scenes.headline: Once Königsberg

scenes.narration: Then the Soviet Union broke up, and Kaliningrad was left stranded behind brand new borders.
scenes.headline: Stranded in 1991

scenes.narration: Even today, going there by land from mainland Russia means passing through other countries.
scenes.headline: Pass Through Others

scenes.narration: That is why many travellers choose to fly or sail there instead.
scenes.headline: Fly Or Sail

scenes.narration: The lesson of this list: borders follow history first, and common sense almost never.
scenes.headline: History Beats Sense

scenes.narration: But Kaliningrad is a whole region. The next place is one small town that lives by two sets of rules.
scenes.headline: Next: One Town

scenes.narration: Number five: Büsingen, a German town sitting inside Switzerland, with Swiss land all around it.
scenes.headline: Büsingen

scenes.narration: Walk out of the town in almost any direction, and you step straight into Switzerland.
scenes.headline: Swiss All Around

scenes.narration: The town is small enough to walk across, yet it has its own German mayor and council.
scenes.headline: Tiny German Town

scenes.narration: Cars here carry their own number plate code, BÜS, so everyone knows they belong to this one town.
scenes.headline: Plate Code BÜS

scenes.narration: Shops accept euros, but Swiss francs are used a lot too, because the town sits inside the Swiss customs area.
scenes.headline: Euros And Francs

scenes.narration: Its landline phone numbers start with the Swiss country code, even though the town is German.
scenes.headline: Swiss Phone Numbers

scenes.narration: On paper it is German. In daily life, it behaves a lot like Switzerland.
scenes.headline: German On Paper

scenes.narration: In 1918, most residents voted to join Switzerland, but the Swiss could not offer anything in exchange.
scenes.headline: Voted To Leave

scenes.narration: So the town stayed German, stuck forever on the wrong side of the line.
scenes.headline: Stuck For Good

scenes.narration: That was a town. The next one is a Spanish town inside France, and it exists because of one word.
scenes.headline: One Word Did It

scenes.narration: Number four: Llívia, a Spanish town sitting inside France.
scenes.headline: Llívia

scenes.narration: On the map, it is a small Spanish dot with French land all around it, a short way from Spain itself.
scenes.headline: Spanish Dot In France

scenes.narration: The reason goes back to a treaty in 1659, when Spain handed France a list of villages in the Pyrenees.
scenes.headline: Treaty Of 1659

scenes.narration: Llívia was once the capital of its valley, so it was officially a town, not a village, and it was not on the list.
scenes.headline: Town, Not Village

scenes.narration: That one word is why a Spanish place sits inside France more than 350 years later.
scenes.headline: One Word, 350 Years

scenes.narration: A short road links it to Spain. It runs over French land, but Spanish travellers are allowed to use it.
scenes.headline: The Neutral Road

scenes.narration: So you can drive from Spain to a Spanish town, and spend part of the journey in France.
scenes.headline: Drive Through France

scenes.narration: Today, people move between France and Llívia without passport checks, because both countries share the Schengen area.
scenes.headline: No Passport Checks

scenes.narration: Now it gets harder to follow. The next place is a piece of one country, inside another, with a third piece inside that.
scenes.headline: It Gets Stranger

scenes.narration: Number three: Madha, a small area of Oman that sits inside the United Arab Emirates.
scenes.headline: Madha

scenes.narration: Look at the map and you see Omani land with the UAE on every side.
scenes.headline: Oman Inside UAE

scenes.narration: And inside Madha there is another surprise: a village called Nahwa, which belongs to the UAE.
scenes.headline: Nahwa Inside Madha

scenes.narration: So you get the UAE, then Oman inside it, then the UAE again inside that.
scenes.headline: Country Dolls

scenes.narration: Think of nesting dolls, except every doll is a piece of a different country.
scenes.headline: Nesting Dolls

scenes.narration: On a map app, you can zoom in and see the border line wrapping around Nahwa like a small circle.
scenes.headline: Zoom In And See

scenes.narration: Why does this exist? Local tribes were loyal to different rulers, and the borders followed those loyalties, not neat lines.
scenes.headline: Borders Follow People

scenes.narration: Remember that idea: borders that follow people, not maps. It matters for the next two places.
scenes.headline: People Not Maps

scenes.narration: If you enjoy strange places like these, subscribe, because there are more of them coming.
scenes.headline: Subscribe For More

scenes.narration: Because number two sits in a valley where three countries are tangled together like a ball of wool.
scenes.headline: Tangled Valley

scenes.narration: Number two: Sokh, in the Fergana Valley of Central Asia.
scenes.headline: Sokh

scenes.narration: On the map, Sokh is an Uzbek enclave, and Kyrgyz land surrounds it on every side.
scenes.headline: Uzbek Enclave

scenes.narration: This is not a tiny hamlet. Tens of thousands of people live there.
scenes.headline: Tens Of Thousands

scenes.narration: Most of them speak Tajik, so you get Tajik speakers, holding Uzbek citizenship, living inside Kyrgyzstan.
scenes.headline: Three Peoples

scenes.narration: Three countries share this valley: Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.
scenes.headline: Three Countries

scenes.narration: The lines were drawn in the Soviet era, when they were only lines inside one big country.
scenes.headline: Soviet Lines

scenes.narration: Then in 1991 those inside lines turned into real international borders almost overnight.
scenes.headline: Overnight Borders

scenes.narration: And Sokh is not alone. The valley has several pockets like it, belonging to different countries.
scenes.headline: Several Pockets

scenes.narration: Tajikistan has a pocket called Vorukh, and Uzbekistan has another called Shakhimardan, both surrounded by Kyrgyz land.
scenes.headline: Vorukh And Shakhimardan

scenes.narration: To reach the rest of Uzbekistan from Sokh, you have to cross Kyrgyz land first.
scenes.headline: Cross Kyrgyz Land

scenes.narration: Water, roads and grazing land have caused real clashes between villagers in this valley.
scenes.headline: Fights Over Water

scenes.narration: Sokh shows what happens when a map is drawn for one country, and then used by three.
scenes.headline: One Map, Three Nations

scenes.narration: Now for number one, the one I promised. It is in India, and the people there lived stuck between two countries.
scenes.headline: Number One Is India

scenes.narration: Number one: the Cooch Behar enclaves, where India and Bangladesh were tangled together like spaghetti.
scenes.headline: Cooch Behar

scenes.narration: Before 2015, Indian plots sat inside Bangladesh, and Bangladeshi plots sat inside India.
scenes.headline: Plots Inside Plots

scenes.narration: Old maps of this area look like a torn sheet of paper, with tiny shapes scattered everywhere.
scenes.headline: A Torn Patchwork

scenes.narration: Many of those plots came from old land deals between local rulers, centuries ago.
scenes.headline: Old Land Deals

scenes.narration: Some were just a few farm fields, and one field could be India while the next was Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: Fields, Two Countries

scenes.narration: In 2015, India gave 111 enclaves to Bangladesh, and Bangladesh gave 51 to India.
scenes.headline: 111 And 51

scenes.narration: That is 162 pockets of land, all settled at midnight on a single night in July.
scenes.headline: 162 Pockets, One Night

scenes.narration: Now the really strange part. Some enclaves sat inside other enclaves.
scenes.headline: Enclaves In Enclaves

scenes.narration: Picture an Indian plot, inside a Bangladeshi plot, inside an Indian plot, inside Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: Four Layers

scenes.narration: At the centre was Dahala Khagrabari, known as the only third-level enclave in the world.
scenes.headline: Dahala Khagrabari

scenes.narration: People there held one country's papers, but every step outside their plot meant walking through another country.
scenes.headline: Papers Of One Country

scenes.narration: Reports from the time said many residents struggled to get schools, electricity and hospitals nearby.
scenes.headline: Hard To Get Help

scenes.narration: In 2015, India and Bangladesh finally signed the deal and cleaned up these lines.
scenes.headline: The Deal In 2015

scenes.narration: Residents were allowed to choose which country they wanted to belong to.
scenes.headline: Choose Your Country

scenes.narration: For many families, it meant a proper address, a school and a vote, maybe for the first time.
scenes.headline: A Proper Address

scenes.narration: So India's strangest border is one that no longer exists, and it ended with a signature, not a war.
scenes.headline: Ended By Signature

scenes.narration: That is six borders that make no sense, from a Russian region cut off from Russia to the tangled fields of Cooch Behar.
scenes.headline: Six Borders Done

scenes.narration: And back in the Fergana Valley, Sokh is still there, still Uzbek, with Kyrgyz land all around it.
scenes.headline: Sokh Still Stands

scenes.narration: Open your map app, search the Fergana Valley, and zoom in. You can see these pockets for yourself.
scenes.headline: See It Yourself

scenes.narration: Your passport can say Uzbekistan while every road around you is in Kyrgyzstan, and it is true.
scenes.headline: Still True

scenes.narration: Next video: more places on the map that look like mistakes, but are completely real.
scenes.headline: Next Video
